I will experience 2 other NDEs in my lifetime: the second one at 38 years old and the third one two days before my 39th birthday. These experiences are shared separately. At a very young age, I was diagnosed with acute rheumatic fever following a severe Streptococcus microbial infection. This inflammatory disease mostly affected my cardiovascular system resulting in valve damages and an enlarged heart. Doctors strongly recommended to my parents that I have my tonsils surgically removed as a preventative measure. This was back in 1959, well before the advent of our universal health care system in Canada. Not having much money, my parents had to shop around to find the lowest price for this surgery. My father never had a car so my parents and I used public transportation to get to the 'clinic' to have my tonsils removed that fateful day. Upon arrival, I noticed that many children were sitting with their parents in the waiting room. As the awful smell of ether forebode an imminent danger, our mournful cries were our last desperate attempt to convince them to return home and forego such a frightful and insane scheme. Innocently, we thought that we would be subjected to yet another inoculation. But what was to come would be far more traumatic than a mere vaccination. A nurse entered the room and called a few names. I prayed that mine would never be pronounced, but in vain. I begged my parents to immediately go back home. Instead, they accompanied me (or rather dragged me) to a small room where they took off my clothes, dressed me in a sterile gown and placed me on a stretcher. The nurse came back in and gave me an injection to calm me down. The smell of ether was getting more and more intense. This was a sure sign that the worst was yet to come. Another nurse entered the room and told my parents to return to the waiting room. The nurse walked over to the head of the stretcher, disengaged the brake and wheeled me to the operating room. I held back my tears because we all know that 'boys don't cry'. I was all alone in the world to face the surgery. After entering the room, I was immediately transferred onto a hard table. A rubber mask was abruptly placed over my face and I was forced to breathe the suffocating odor of chloroform gas. I tried to struggle but my body was unresponsive. My eyelids became heavier and then nothingness. Suddenly, I felt myself floating face down over my body and rising up towards the ceiling as an unusual feeling of great peace and well-being overwhelmed me. I noticed three masked individuals in surgical gowns standing below me. They were leaning over a long table and seemed quite upset and agitated. There was a sort of humming sound in my ears so I couldn’t hear their conversation. The door flew open and a fourth individual in garbs came running in. He appeared quite irritated and was yelling at the others. I still couldn't hear a thing as the humming noise was getting even louder. Was I dreaming? If so, never had I experienced such a marvelous dream filled with serenity, joy and love so intense that mere words cannot describe. These powerful emotions were new to me and yet, they felt so very familiar. Without any fear or concern, I floated to the other side of the room. I noticed a child lying on the table. As I took a closer look, I realized that it was me! I was in no way shocked or terrified by this awareness, quite the contrary. I felt very euphoric as it seemed to be a normal phenomenon and even a joyous and sublime omen. The humming in my ears intensified. It suddenly stopped when a long and upward dark tunnel appeared behind me at about a 45-degree angle. I saw a bright white light glowing at its furthest point. It was like standing at one end of a long train tunnel and staring at the beam of light from the locomotive entering at the other end. I felt a pulling force as an energy was beckoning me to enter the vortex. Without any fear or hesitation, I slowly floated towards its entrance. I was overwhelmed with feelings of Happiness, peace, unconditional love and excitement. It was as though I was returning home after a long trip abroad, eagerly looking forward to reuniting again with family and dear friends. I made my way through the tunnel with increasing speed in a clockwise spiral motion. I heard sublime music which no words can describe. It could be compared with the most beautiful classical music ever composed. My eyes easily fill with tears when I relive that mystic experience listening to specific musical pieces composed by classical masters. As I got closer to the light, I felt intense feelings of unconditional love and exceptional peace. I could stare directly at its brilliance even though it seemed far brighter than when looking directly at the sun. I had no sorrow nor regret for having been 'taken away' from my parents, my brother and others whom I love as I knew for sure that I was still constantly with them. Suddenly, I came to a standstill and was promptly pushed away in the opposite direction at a dizzying speed. I excruciatingly reintegrating the little boy’s body on the operation table. As I opened my eyes in the recovery room, a terrible torment invaded my whole body and my throat seemed to be on fire. My mother was at my bedside with tears in her eyes. The white sheets were covered with blood. With unbearable pain, I repeatedly vomited blood. How I wished I could instantly return to my marvelous 'dream' where I was completely freed of my sorrow and pain. I implored my mother that we return home. She answered that the doctor wanted to keep me under observation for a while longer. Later that evening, the doctor finally told my parents that we could go home although I was still quite feverish and still vomiting blood. My father called for a taxi. Noticing my condition, the taxi driver placed some newspapers on the car’s floor to protect it. Up until my teenage years, I thought that my out-of-body experience had only been a dream or an hallucination although it still remained quite fresh in my mind throughout all those years. Even now writing these lines, my eyes fill with tears as these memories still have a powerful effect on me. I experienced 2 other NDEs in my lifetime: the first one at 7 years old and the third one two days before my 39th birthday. I was born with a heart disease named Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) Syndrome. It is characterized by the presence of an additional conductive pathway between the auricle and the ventricle. Since early childhood, this illness would bring about tachyarrhythmia symptoms at irregular intervals. These episodes could last from a few minutes up to a couple of hours. The manifestations would eventually subside and stop without medication. A few years had passed since my last tachyarrhythmia episode but this was about to change quite radically. On that day, I was at the office writing reports after a week of conducting inspections. I chose this particular weekday to work from our downtown Montreal office as I would be teaching an evening class at a nearby college. Much to my surprise, I started experiencing increased and irregular heartbeats in mid-afternoon. At 5 PM, the tachyarrhythmia episode continued as I drove to the college. It was still ongoing at 6 PM when I started my lecture. At the 7:30 PM break, I felt totally exhausted from my heart’s continued marathon. I called my wife Lucy to inform her of my symptoms and ask her to come meet me at the college so she could drive me back home. She arrived at 8 PM but I stubbornly carried on with my lecture until the usual time of 9 PM when she entered the classroom with a furious look on her face. She couldn’t believe that I had insisted on completing the class in spite of my condition. Once in the car, I told her that it would be safer to stop at the hospital. She dropped me off at the emergency entrance door before making her way to the parking lot. Dressed in a business suit, I entered the emergency room where some twenty people were seated. After explaining my symptoms and condition to the receptionist, she told me to take a seat and that a triage nurse would come see me. I noticed a big fellow pacing up and down the aisle and holding onto his right hand that was wrapped in a bloodied bandage. He seemed furious and kept cursing out loud. A nurse entered the room calling my name. As I got up, she insisted that I remain seated. She tried to take my pulse but to no avail. My heartbeats were so fast and irregular that she couldn’t get an exact reading. With a worried look, she asked me if I could follow her to an exam room. As I stood up, the big fellow yelled and swore at her complaining that he had been waiting for three long hours to see a doctor whereas I had just arrived and was being promptly looked after. With a strong voice she told him to shut-up and sit down. Entering the exam room, the nurse insisted that I immediately lie down on the bed. A doctor shortly came in to question me. I told him about my WPW Syndrome and that the tachyarrhythmia symptoms had begun at around 3 PM. Seeming a bit confused, he returned to his desk which I could easily see. After some talk with colleagues, they each took a book and began flipping the pages. It appeared to me that they were not readily knowledgeable about this uncommon cardiac illness. Suddenly one of them shouted out I found it! Wolff-Parkinson-White. Lucy had just entered the emergency room and was searching for me. She immediately knew where to go upon hearing these words. A few minutes later, the attending doctor told us that he had phoned the head cardiologist to discuss my case. I had to stay the night in the ER to receive an intravenous (IV) perfusion of Pronestyl, a powerful antiarrhythmic medication. Lucy returned home to get some rest and would return early the next morning. Three IV bags of Pronestyl were perfused during that night but to no avail. I was sleepless not only because of the ER hectic activity but also due to my heart's continuous marathon and the urge to urinate several times an hour. The heart rate monitor was in a constant frenzy: 195 beats per minute (BPM), 240, 315, 190, etc. My heartbeats were so fast and irregular that it couldn’t get an exact pulse. Some nurses told me that they had never experienced such symptoms and effects before. I was the talk of the nurses’ station when as each new shift arrived. The head cardiologist arrived at 9 AM. Eighteen hours had passed since my symptoms began. I had not slept for some thirty hours. He informed me that the antiarrhythmic medication had no results whatsoever in spite of its high dosage. He asked me if I was ever a smoker. I said no and inquired why. He told me that, had I been a smoker, my heart would have probably failed under such a strain. With a concerned look on his face, he added that it was crucial to put an end to this crisis without further delay. The only remaining option was to proceed with an electrical cardioversion in order to attempt to restore my heart's normal rhythm. He explained that this approach consisted of placing two electrodes on the skin over the rib cage and sending an electrical impulse through the body, towards the heart. This electrical discharge would interrupt the atrial fibrillation and restore the heart’s normal rhythm. My immediate reply was: In other words, it is a controlled electrocution. He gave me a smile and nodded his head in agreement. I asked him if there were any other options. Not really was his answer. I told him that I would discuss it with my wife as soon as she arrived. He insisted that there was no time to lose and that he had already ordered the set-up at the intensive care unit (ICU) where I would be brought to in a few minutes. Lucy hurriedly entered the ICU shortly followed by the head cardiologist. I told him that I'd like to give a call to my personal cardiologist to get his opinion about this course of action. With a commanding tone of voice, he answered that it was HIS decision to make and that it would be too risky to further delay the procedure. He then asked Lucy to leave and wait in the hallway. As she left, he informed me that I would be given a sedative. A few seconds later, I was unconscious. Suddenly, I felt myself floating face down over my body and rising up towards the ceiling. A familiar tunnel, at 45-degree angle, opened up behind me as I calmly watched several cardioversion attempts by the medical team below. Without any hesitation, I surrendered to its attracting vortex. It was exactly as I had first experienced it at seven years old. Once again, I was overwhelmed with feelings of Happiness, peace, unconditional love and excitement. It was as though I was returning home after a long trip abroad, eagerly looking forward to reuniting again with family and dear friends. Spirally travelling through the tunnel, in a clockwise manner, and approaching its majestic and soothing white light beckoning me, I abruptly came to a standstill. A choice was proposed to me. Either I continue on and enter the light or I immediately return to my earthly body. I had no such option thirty years ago at the time of my first near death experience. Nor will it be offered in October of next year in the event of my third NDE. I still cannot explain exactly how this information was communicated to me nor by whom. I believe that it was telepathically conveyed by a spirit guide. It's as though I was offered the possibility of extending my earthly stay in this lifetime in order to carry out future tasks or missions. Strangely, I could hear Lucy's voice strongly urging me to take very deep breaths. I was immediately hurled back through the tunnel at lightning speed and painfully re-entered my body. As I slowly regained consciousness and opened my eyes, I could see her standing at my bedside accompanied by the head cardiologist, the anesthesiologist and a nurse. I felt an excruciating chest pain with a terrible burning sensation. I had endured some intense sunburns in my life but they seemed trivial compared with this particular trauma. It was like I had been scorched by a flaming torch. A smell of roasted chicken permeated the room. Later that morning, Lucy told me that a nurse had hurriedly rushed out of the ICU and insisted that she quickly follow her. Once at my bedside, the head cardiologist instructed her to firmly and repeatedly tell me to take deep breaths as my breathing was too shallow due to my deep exhaustion. Later that day, he informed me that several electric shocks were needed to finally obtain a normal heart rhythm. This clearly explained the intense chest pain and burning sensation I was experiencing as well as the roasted chicken I smelled. Just after dawn on the following morning, I was taken by ambulance to the cardiology unit of a specialized hospital for a thorough exam. The objective was to find an effective treatment capable of stopping any future tachyarrhythmia episode. Unfortunately, after a long and tiresome exam, it was determined that no available medication could succeed in doing so in my personal case. In other words, urgent electrical cardioversion would be the only way to interrupt any future tachyarrhythmia episode and regain my heart’s normal rhythm. Nonetheless, Pronestyl pills were prescribed to be taken if necessary. The next occurrence would be in September of the following year and it would be more life threatening. It happened during a grueling yearly five-day business trip to Abitibi (northwestern Quebec) and Timmins (northeastern Ontario) where there are no cardiology units nor cardiologists in hospitals. Once I had returned home with difficulty, I had an appointment with a cardiac surgeon who strongly recommended urgent open-heart surgery fearing that, otherwise, the tachyarrhythmia episodes could increase in frequency. I experienced my third NDE during this complex invasive surgery.
